summary:
Lima stands under the national framework of Peru: trans identity is not criminalised, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising. The Metropolitan Municipality of Lima sets none of these rules itself; a trans visitor to the capital is governed by national statute and by the enforcement practice of national agencies and private security operating in the city.

On 20 February 2025 the Congressional Women and Family Commission approved unanimously, for plenary debate, a bill barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex that does not match their biological sex at birth. The same text obliges public premises to remove "ambiguous" signage of the kind Jorge Chávez international airport had displayed, wording such as "for all persons with female identity" and "for all persons with male identity". The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents then mandated that restroom entry be determined by biological sex, extending the bar to trans youth, and the wider legislative package bans inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity".

Enforcement is expected to reach individuals at the door. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho warns that the restriction will be applied through identity-card (DNI) checks carried out by security staff deciding who may enter a restroom, a screening practice she describes as discriminatory and grounded in prejudice rather than in any observed conduct.

Violence against trans people in Peru is documented and under-recorded. An Observatory report covering 2020 to 2023 counted 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reported rights violations, with trans women the most affected group at 30 of the 54 killed; 19 homicides were recorded in 2023 alone, and in 26 of the killings no suspects were identified. The state maintains no system recording the sexual orientation or gender identity of victims of killing, so official counts understate the pattern.

The capital illustrates that pattern. On 12 February 2023 members of the "Los Gallegos" gang kidnapped trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, from jirón Chancay in central Lima; she was killed with roughly 30 gunshots.
tangentialFactors:
Peru remains without LGBT coverage in its hate-crime law: Congress voted in 2017 to strip those protections from the new Penal Code, leaving Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking such coverage. Hate-crime reporting in Lima therefore has no specific statutory hook.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The bathroom statute and the removal of inclusive signage sit in tension with that binding regional standard, and the same Court has jurisdiction over cases arising from Lima.

In December 2025 three police officers were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court's first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Speech and association are constrained nationally: vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including a ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Lima live under the April 2025 restroom rule in schools, clinics, shopping centres and workplaces, and the obligation to remove "ambiguous" signage binds premises across the metropolitan area. Reporting a discriminatory sign or a DNI check at a restroom door has no hate-crime provision to invoke, since LGBT protections were removed from the Penal Code in 2017.

The IDEHPUCP institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru found that the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity and implicitly framing them as harassment risks; it also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, indicating the limited recourse available through administrative channels.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 report on rising hate crimes and a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stresses that recorded figures are only a sub-registry of actual incidence.
outOfScopeNotes:
How the April 2025 restroom mandate is applied in practice across Lima's municipal facilities is not sourced here: the inventory does not record signage audits, security-briefing directives, or any enforcement action taken by the Metropolitan Municipality of Lima itself.

Whether the DNI-check screening described by Gianna Camacho has in fact been carried out at any specific Lima venue remains unresolved; her statement is a warning about how enforcement will operate, not a documented incident.

The 170 reported rights violations recorded for 2020 to 2023 are national totals and are not broken down for Lima in this inventory, so the capital's share of that count is unresolved. The same applies to the 19 homicides recorded in 2023 and to the 26 killings without identified suspects.

Whether Rubí Torres Silvano's killing has resulted in convictions, and its current status before the Peruvian courts, is not stated in the sources and is unresolved.

The interaction between the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 and the domestic restroom statute has not been litigated in Lima, so far as this inventory records.
